item.title: Brown Tree Snake Working Group to sign agreement to eradicate snakes from Cocos Island

item.content:encoded:
Members of the Brown Tree Snake Technical Working Group are preparing to sign a memorandum of understanding aimed at eradicating invasive brown tree snakes from Islan Dåno’, also known as Cocos Island.

The signing is scheduled for Nov. 17, during the group’s annual public meeting at the Hilton Guam Resort and Spa. The agreement formalizes six years of efforts to eliminate the snakes from the island through collaboration among local conservation organizations, nonprofit groups, the Government of Guam, and federal agencies.

A breeding population of brown tree snakes was discovered on Dåno’ in 2020, prompting independent efforts to remove the invasive species. Organizers say the goal is to achieve complete eradication, which would mark the first successful removal of an invasive snake from an island anywhere in the world.

Dåno’ is home to the only wild population of ko’ko’, or Guam rails, which disappeared from Guam due to brown tree snake predation. The snakes have had significant ecological and economic impacts on Guam and remain a threat to neighboring islands.

The annual meeting will also feature updates on brown tree snake research, management, and eradication efforts. Organizers say this year’s work has been particularly demanding following three typhoons and two brown tree snake sightings on Rota after Typhoon Bavi.

The public meeting runs from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the memorandum signing scheduled for 12:20 p.m. in the Micronesian Room at the Hilton Guam Resort and Spa.

The event is free and open to the public.

item.title: Solar developer to recruit up to 150 workers across CNMI
item.description: Appearing virtually before the Commonwealth Utilities Corp. board Thursday, Eastern Power Solutions Chief Executive Officer Daniel Myung said the company has started recruiting between 100 and 150 workers and intends to hire residents from Saipan, Tinian and Rota as it advances development of its renewable energy projects across the Commonwealth. Responding to concerns raised by CUC board member M
item.content:encoded:
Appearing virtually before the Commonwealth Utilities Corp. board Thursday, Eastern Power Solutions Chief Executive Officer Daniel Myung said the company has started recruiting between 100 and 150 workers and intends to hire residents from Saipan, Tinian and Rota as it advances development of its renewable energy projects across the Commonwealth.

Responding to concerns raised by CUC board member Miranda Manglona about equitable hiring among the islands, Myung said the company plans to recruit locally on each island and establish training programs in Saipan, Tinian and Rota.

"We would prefer to have Rota projects done as much as possible through Rota residents, and Tinian projects done through Tinian residents," Myung said. "Rather than transporting our workers back and forth, it makes sense to work with the local people there."

Myung said Eastern Power Solutions has already hired key personnel, including a chief engineer, and recently advertised positions as it ramps up staffing for project implementation.

The company is also moving forward with environmental reviews and financing requirements. Myung said EPS has initiated the National Environmental Policy Act process with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, completed preliminary surveys and is finalizing documentation for a USDA loan.

According to Myung, the company expects to complete the solar generation component of the project by December 2027, place the battery energy storage system into service by September 2028 and fully commission the integrated system by December 2028.

item.title: Interior Department announces $450 million in fiscal 2027 Compact funding for Palau, FSM, Marshall Islands
item.description: The U.S. Department of the Interior announced $450 million in fiscal 2027 funding for Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands. The money comes from the Compact of Free Association Amendments Act of 2023, which updated agreements between the U.S. and the three nations.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of the Interior announced $450 million in fiscal 2027 funding for Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.

The money comes from the Compact of Free Association Amendments Act of 2023, which updated agreements between the U.S. and the three nations.

Palau gets than $41 million to support health care, education, infrastructure projects, the Infrastructure Maintenance Fund and the Fiscal Consolidation Fund.

The Federated States of Micronesia gets $140 million to support health, education, infrastructure, environmental programs, private sector development and capacity building.

The Marshall Islands gets more than $171 million to support payments to Kwajalein landowners, health care, education, environmental programs, capacity building, the U.S. Supplemental Health Fund and improved financial reporting and accountability.

The Republic of the Marshall Islands will also receive $100 million as the final U.S. contribution to its Compact Trust Fund, which supports the nation's long-term fiscal self-reliance.

The Department of the Interior says it will continue to oversee compact assistance to promote accountability, responsible investment and improved public services across the freely associated states.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
item.description: Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children. The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.
item.content:encoded:
Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children. The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027.

There had been speculation that the mistrial of her first trial might spur prosecutors to consider lesser charges that wouldn't require a jury, such as manslaughter or second-degree murder. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.

"Given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Mass.

In response, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated, "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."

Judge Sullivan is expected to preside over the new trial. He oversaw Clancy's murder trial that ended in a mistrial two months ago.

The decision to retry Clancy emerges after the judge denied a request from Clancy's defense team to dismiss the criminal charges against her on double jeopardy grounds.

Clancy's defense has argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her young children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

Clancy was initially tried on three charges of first-degree murder, one for each of her children. Her case has drawn intense media interest, due to the shocking killings of her young children. And as WBUR has reported , the trial has also sparked conspiracy theories online.

Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4, after five weeks of testimony and seven days of jury deliberations. The jurors, nine women and three men, repeatedly told Sullivan they were deadlocked , unable to reach a unanimous decision. Jurors said a lone juror refused to join 11 others in finding Clancy not guilty of murder.

Clancy's defense filed several motions after the mistrial. The first asked the court to issue a "required finding of not guilty," a Massachusetts state law term for instances where judges determine there's insufficient evidence to sustain a conviction. Another focused on the holdout juror, asking the court for an inquiry and to examine their responses to a juror questionnaire and other records. Sullivan denied both of those motions .

When deliberations were dragging out at the end of the trial, Reddington had asked the judge to remove the holdout juror, saying the jury foreperson reported one juror refused to follow the law in regards to reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to dismiss the juror, saying he reaffirmed his instructions with all the jurors about the law.

Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. But her attorneys didn't deny that she killed her three children in January of 2023. Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were found strangled in the basement of the home Clancy shared with her then-husband Patrick in Duxbury, Mass., south of Boston.

In court, Clancy's defense argued that she can't be held criminally liable because of her mental state at the time of the killings. Her attorney said Clancy was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis, and didn't get adequate mental health help when she sought it out.

"I'm appalled and disgusted," Reddington said of Clancy's medical care, as NPR and WBUR reported . "It's repulsive what happened here."

But prosecutors argued Clancy was mentally capable of committing a premeditated crime, accusing her of sending her husband out on errands so she would be alone with their children. And they raised doubts about Clancy's claims that a voice told her to kill them.

"This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said in her closing statement. "That's a distraction to get you angry and passionate about an important issue, but an issue that's not on trial here."

During the trial, the jury visited the house where the Clancy children died. Their bus route also took them past two places Patrick Clancy visited that evening — a CVS and a takeout restaurant -- before returning home to a horrific scene. Sullivan told the jurors that the visit, called a "view" under Massachusetts state law, was meant to "help you better understand the evidence" by seeing the locations and the house's layout.

Clancy remains in the custody of a state psychiatric hospital where she's been held for more than three years. She was severely injured by attempts to end her own life, and she used a wheelchair during the trial.

Massachusetts' highest court recently reversed a conviction in a separate case involving a mother killing her children – a case that both Cruz, the prosecutor, and Sullivan, the judge, also worked on.

In August, the state Supreme Judicial Court ordered a new trial for Latarsha Sanders, saying Sullivan committed an error in not allowing the jury to see medical records documenting Sanders' mental illness after she was arrested. Sanders was convicted of murder in 2022; she had argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she suffered a psychotic episode.

item.title: RAYE and Rosalía lead the 2027 Grammy nominations

item.content:encoded:
The nominations for the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced on Monday, and women artists across genres dominate the major categories.

The British singer-songwriter RAYE, whose breakthrough song "Where Is My Husband!" was a hit on the pop charts as well as social media feeds over the past year, leads the field with 11 nominations. That ties a record Beyoncé set in 2025 for the number of nominations earned by a woman artist in a single year. "Husband!" is up for record and song of the year, and RAYE's This Music May Contain Hope. is nominated for album of the year.

The Spanish artist Rosalía, whose classical-influenced album Lux features the artist singing in 14 languages on songs that span a number of genres, comes in second place for most nominations, racking up nine nods. Rosalía, who took home song of the year and album of the year at the Latin Grammys just last week, has only been nominated four times at the Grammys. She has won twice in the Latin rock or alternative album category. This year, her nominations come in album, song and record of the year, plus pop, alternative, Latin and global categories.

Other artists picking up major nominations include the breakout country star and best new artist nominee Ella Langley, whose "Choosin' Texas" recently broke the record as the longest-running No. 1 song in the history of the Billboard pop chart — it has held the top spot for 27 weeks already this year. Langley and veteran country star Miranda Lambert, who co-wrote "Choosin' Texas," both scored seven nominations. Also with seven nominations is a pair of rock-leaning singer-songwriters: Olivia Rodrigo's third album, You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, is up for album of the year, as is Lost Weekend by Phoebe Bridgers. Bridgers, who earned her first Grammy awards in 2024 for her work in the band boygenius, was nominated as best new artist in 2021. Rodrigo won that award in 2022.

Of the eight artists competing for album of the year, only two of them have ever won in the category: Taylor Swift and Bruno Mars (who is the only male artist up for the award this year). Along with a genre-diverse mix of names up for best new artist — including New York rock darlings Geese, the experimental rock band Angine de Poitrine and alt-pop star Slayyyter — it's an eclectic list of nominations for the Grammys, which are scheduled to be presented in Los Angeles on Sunday, Feb. 7, 2027.

Read the complete list of nominees below:

6. Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical

38. Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance

item.title: Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case
item.description: Updated November 17, 2026 at 2:06 AM ChST Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that he is gaining momentum in his bid to unseat longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, taking a traditionally private Senate leadership contest into public view.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 17, 2026 at 2:06 AM ChST

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that he is gaining momentum in his bid to unseat longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, taking a traditionally private Senate leadership contest into public view.

"Well, I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here," Van Hollen told NPR's Steve Inskeep on Morning Edition .

Over the weekend, he appeared on CNN, ABC and Fox News to make his case for new Democratic leadership after his party's sweeping midterm victories. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, says he has enough votes to remain leader.

Van Hollen is hardly a Washington outsider. The progressive Democrat has spent nearly 25 years on Capitol Hill, served as a deputy to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and led Democratic campaign efforts in both chambers. He has been a vocal opponent of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development, and he has called for investigations into the administration's foreign aid cuts.

Schumer has continued to support U.S. military assistance to Israel despite his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Van Hollen, by contrast, has pushed to restrict weapons sales and military aid to the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, while pressing for more humanitarian aid to Palestinians.

"I certainly oppose the idea of an American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel, regardless of its actions," Van Hollen said.

Van Hollen also wants Democratic leaders to stay out of contested primaries. He pointed to the victories of incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

"We have two senators-elect who would not be there if the current majority leader had his way," he said.

He described the midterm victories as a populist rejection of President Trump, rather than an election orchestrated by Washington Democrats.

Van Hollen also cited legislation to strengthen labor unions, which never received a vote on the Senate floor. On the war in Iran, he called for an end to further funding.

"We should not be voting for one penny in mid-December to continue this war," he said.

Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win. The election will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, making it difficult to know how many votes either candidate secured.

Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

The digital version of this live interview was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

item.title: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
item.description: Updated November 17, 2026 at 1:15 AM ChST President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 17, 2026 at 1:15 AM ChST

President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.

The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific.

The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen.

The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit. Trump said as he left the White House Monday that he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila.

The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days.

For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together.

"The Chinese strongly disagree with the idea that they should be involved in any kind of trilateral discussions with the United States and Russia on nuclear weapons," Kagan said.

"China wants to avoid this because they don't want to be locked into a subservient position. And they also don't want to create a precedent. I think the main thing for the Chinese is they know if they do a meeting and nuclear issues are discussed, it becomes much harder for them to refuse to do it in the future," he said.

A White House official said they do not expect any agreement to come out of the meeting on denuclearization.

"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said, calling the trilateral an "entry point" for the three countries to talk about reducing nuclear weapons stock.

Another U.S. official not authorized to speak on the record acknowledged that denuclearization is a "difficult" topic for China.

"But we do think it's time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said.

Putin, for his part, stands to benefit from a meeting with Trump and Xi, as Russia's war with Ukraine nears its five-year mark. Trump has made friendlier moves toward Russia in recent months, siding with Putin and striking a deal to release more Russian oil into the market ahead of the midterm elections.

Trump said last month that he was fine with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not being present at a potential meeting with Putin about the war.

"Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said.

A White House official said Ukraine is not intended to come up in the meeting with Xi and Putin. And there is no plan for Putin and Trump to have a separate meeting.

But Trump said Monday he would be talking about his "favorite subject Ukraine."

Kagan said the meeting with Xi, Trump and Putin could end up being on the shorter side if there isn't much all parties are willing to discuss. But at the same time, "I could see this going longer because President Trump likes dealing with Putin and Xi. He sees them as his peers. He sees them as important world leaders," Kagan said.

Either way, a photo of the three leaders meeting together is enough to make headlines.

"That picture alone is going to be worth well over a thousand words," Kagan said.

This is the second time Trump and Xi are meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit – but this year's meeting is notably different from last year's in Busan, South Korea, when tensions between the US and China were fraught amid the escalating trade war.

The meeting in Busan established a sort-of truce between the two countries. The U.S. immediately lowered some tariffs on Chinese goods and China agreed to loosen exports on rare earths. But the execution of the agreement has been spotty.

"There's friction in this truce. It's not smooth, but it's basically functional," Kurt Tong, Managing Partner at The Asia Group, said.

A White House official said the U.S. isn't getting rare earths from China at the pace or level they'd like.

"We really want to focus minds among our counterparts in China on compliance with this," they said.

Still, Tong expects the agreement to be renewed past its January expiration. The two sides will likely agree to the renewal either in Shenzhen or later this year at the G20 summit Trump is hosting in Miami, according to Tong.

Before the president arrives in China, he's holding meetings with several allies in Manila, including a meeting with the other leaders of the Quad nations: India, Japan and Australia.
